Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Baltimore MD/Washington DC
326 PM EST Tue Nov 24 2026

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...
The latest guidance continues to increase confidence in wet and
windy conditions for Thanksgiving. Rain showers, possibly mixed
with a little snow, could trek east of the mountains Friday.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
- 1) Colder than normal temperatures precede a powerful East
  Coast storm for the Thanksgiving holiday.

- 2) Seasonable temperatures and drier conditions this weekend
  with additional rain chances early next week.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
KEY MESSAGE 1...Colder than normal temperatures precede a powerful 
East Coast storm for the Thanksgiving holiday.

North to northeast winds will accompany a near record strong
(for November) area of high pressure pivoting into northern New
England through tonight. Winds will begin to increase Wednesday
as low pressure takes shape off the Southeast coast. Anticipate
below normal temperatures tonight, with calm winds and clear
skies resulting in ideal radiational cooling for the northern
Shenandoah Valley vicinity with teens possible by daybreak.
Elsewhere, lows will be in the 20s to around freezing, perhaps a
tick above freezing in the major city centers. Some high clouds
approaching from the south late could offset cooling near and
south of I-64, with light winds north of US-50 and east of the
Catoctins similarly inhibiting full radiational cooling there.

Abundant clouds are expected to move over the area by nightfall
Wednesday following a seasonable day. A trio of shortwaves will
approach from the west and south. A northern stream upper-level
low over the MS Valley will dig into the OH Valley. A lead wave
in the southern stream will lift from the Caribbean toward FL, 
and a trailing southern stream wave will shift across the 
southern Plains into the Southeast. The southern stream waves 
will phase, with their eastward progress blocked by strong high 
pressure anchored near the Canadian Maritimes. Despite the 
strength of the high (~1045 mb), a lack of a deeper connection 
to the northern stream leading into this storm means cold air 
will be largely absent by the time precipitation arrives, 
especially given the strong advection of an airmass with 
tropical origins into the region.

One exception could be above about 3800 feet in eastern WV where
near freezing temperatures could linger, supporting some minor
snow or ice early Thursday.

The two phased southern stream waves will induce surface low 
development near the Carolinas, which will then pivot northward 
in meridional flow east of the OH Valley upper low. Most progs
show a sub-1000 mb low moving northward up the coast as the
1040+ mb high to the north only slowly relents. This results in 
an extreme gradient and aims an intense low-level jet at the
East Coast, reaching the Mid-Atlantic by Thanksgiving morning.

The result will be a large area of moderately heavy rain, highly
efficient given the extreme moisture transport and highly
anomalous PWs of 1.2-1.6". Despite generally weak lapse rates
aloft, the very strong dynamic lift coupled with the increase in
moisture could result in enough elevated instability for a few
claps of thunder, mainly near and east of the low track (which
looks to be roughly near I-95, give or take 25-50 miles
depending on exact location).

Despite the extreme moisture parameters in place, recent drought
as well as the relatively progressive nature of the system
should limit the duration and impact of heavy rain, with only
very limited flooding potential. The modest instability should
also keep rainfall rates generally 0.2-0.4" per hour, though
some 1" per hour rates are possible in heavier elements/bands.
Total rainfall amounts of 1-3" are expected, with locally 
higher totals to 5" possible in any persistent bands or in 
favorable easterly upslope areas along and east of the Blue 
Ridge and Catoctin Mountains. Although the overall flood risk is
limited, should these higher totals falls over an urban area 
there could be some hydro-related impacts. Additionally, given 
the time of year, leaves may clog storm drains and gutters 
resulting in an uptick of poor drainage ponding.

The intense low-level jet also raises the prospect for gusty to
damaging winds, especially when combined with the rain and wet
ground that will develop. The low levels will be quite stable,
with a stout temperature inversion up to around 5,000 feet 
above the surface. Still, 50 to 80 mph winds will exist in this
layer, so although there will be a significant reduction between
winds a few thousand feet up and the surface, gusts of 30 to 45
mph are still likely across much of the area. Higher gusts (40 
to 55 mph) are anticipated east of US-15 where the gradient 
will be stronger, as well as at higher elevations that poke into
the low-level jet. Higher elevations (as well as areas just 
west of ridges) could experience occasionally localized higher 
gusts around 60 mph if downsloping effects can offset low-level 
stability. There may also be similarly higher gusts with any 
convective elements or gravity waves, as hinted at in some 12Z 
REFS members, again most likely east of US-15 or so (dependent 
on low track). Scattered to numerous instances of downed trees 
and power lines with power outages and other light objects being
blown over can be expected with winds this strong. There is 
still some timing uncertainty, but the strongest winds look to 
move from south to north from just after daybreak to midday 
Thursday, before gradually subsiding through the late afternoon 
and evening hours as the low center lifts to the north. Wind 
direction will be out of the northeast to southeast as the low 
approaches and passes.

If the low tracks far enough inland, the warm sector could
impinge on at least southern MD. In this scenario, some near
surface-based instability would develop on the back end of the
extreme low-level wind field, resulting in a conditional risk
for a severe thunderstorm.

Once the low lifts to the north, the steadier precipitation
shuts off. West to southwest winds may become gusty again, and
as the upper low approaches from the OH Valley upslope showers
will become prevalent. Cooling temperatures aloft should change
rain to snow after midnight Thanksgiving night over the
Alleghenies, and cooler temperatures aloft could be enough to
mix in some wet snowflakes or graupel/snow pellets east of the
mountains as the upper low crosses the lower elevations Friday.
Winds will remain blustery with gusts of 25 to 40 mph.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Seasonable temperatures and drier conditions this 
weekend with additional rain chances early next week.

Upper-level low pressure will work across the region Friday 
while the surface coastal low continues toward southeast Quebec.
Weak mid-level ridging will settle over the region Saturday 
into Sunday as surface high pressure sits off the southeast U.S. 
coast. Blustery conditions will continue as a result with a slow
tapering of the winds as the gradient relaxes late Saturday 
into Sunday. Look for gusts of 30 to 40 mph (locally higher over
the mountains) Friday with 25 to 35 mph gusts Saturday, and 15 
to 25 mph gusts Sunday. Winds will generally be out of the west 
and southwest before turning back to the north and northwest 
early next week.

Outside of the wind, expect upslope rain/snow showers over the 
mountains through Friday night. A few spotty graupel showers may
work their way eastward, although most will remain dry. Any 
snow accumulations over the mountains will be tied to elevations
above 2800 feet given marginal temperature profiles and an
unfavorable wind direction for more efficient upslope to occur.
Still, a burst with the upper low could result in a few inches
on some of the higher ridges.

Dry conditions will prevail with passing wave clouds Saturday 
and Sunday. By late Sunday night into Monday, precipitation 
chances return. 06z/12z models are a bit divergent here in 
regards to the formation of a coastal low and track of a low 
pressure system over the Ohio River Valley along with its 
associated front early next week. The ECMWF and Canadian are 
faster compared to the GFS which is slower and more curtailed to
a system Tuesday into mid next week. Either way, another chance
of widespread measurable rainfall is on the table during the 
November 30th through December 2nd timeframe (whether it be from
one system or a series of systems Sun-Mon and Wed-Thu next 
week; a lack of deeper cold air means rain is favored for now).

What we do know this far out in the back half of the extended is 
that the pattern will remain active. It looks as if we will get into 
a cycle of 2 to 3 dry days followed by precipitation (either from a 
front or coastal system) due in part to an active southern jet and 
meridional flow pattern. Stay tuned for further updates.

Temperatures will remain seasonable with highs in the upper 50s and 
low 60s (mid to upper 40s mountains). Overnight lows will fall back 
into the 30s.

&&

.AVIATION /18Z TUESDAY THROUGH SUNDAY/...
VFR conditions persist through at least Wednesday evening. As 
strong high pressure passes by to the north, expect an increase 
in northeasterly winds during this time. Gradients tighten 
further into Wednesday night ahead of the potent coastal system 
arriving for Thanksgiving Day. Restrictions and strong LLWS become
likely after 03Z Thursday. Waves of rain will arrive from the
south late Wednesday night into Thanksgiving morning bringing a
prolonged period of flight restrictions, likely to IFR. Sporadic
thunder can't be ruled out near the metros. Very gusty surface 
winds 35-45 knots are expected to peak Thursday, as well. Winds 
shift to the west and southwest as VFR returns and precip ends
Thursday night.

VFR to MVFR conditions will return for Friday and Saturday as 
coastal/upper-level low pressure depart the region. Will look 
for MVFR stratocumulus/wave clouds at times for both Friday and
Saturday as a result of downsloping west/southwest flow east of
the mountains. Most terminals will remain dry although a few 
graupel showers are possible east of of the Alleghenies with any
upslope rain/snow shower activity confined to locations west of
a line from CBE-EKN-HSP. LLWS will also remain an issue Friday 
morning into Friday afternoon and potentially again late 
Saturday into Sunday.

VFR conditions will prevail Sunday under brief high pressure before 
sub-VFR conditions return with a series of low pressure systems 
early to mid next week.

&&

.MARINE...
Hazardous conditions are likely to be present over the waterways
for much of the week. After a brief lull, winds increase by late
tonight out of the northeast. By Wednesday, gradients tighten 
further as strong high pressure passes through New England and 
low pressure lifts up from the Gulf Coast. Northeasterly gusts 
up to 20 to 30 knots are expected through Wednesday evening,
with gale conditions possibly as soon as early evening in the
waters off southern Maryland. Easterly gusts of 35 to 45 knots
will spread northward late Wednesday night into Thanksgiving
morning, with gusts around 50 knots possible off southern
Maryland and quite possibly up the main channel of the
Chesapeake Bay if the low track is just to the west. A few
thunderstorms can't be ruled out Thursday, either, though most
of the time will just be steady to heavy rain and wind.

A lull in wind is likely as precipitation ends and the low moves
away Thursday evening, though west to southwest winds on the
back side of the low could again approach 30 to 35 knots by late
Thursday night into Friday. Although they gradually subside, 
winds will remain elevated through Saturday afternoon which 
likely warrants Small Craft Advisories. Additional SCAs may be 
needed Sunday due to channeling. SCAs may linger Monday and 
Tuesday as another low pressure system approaches the waters.

&&

.TIDES/COASTAL FLOODING...
Intense low pressure will move up the coast, with very strong
(near record) high pressure to the north. This results in a
period of strong onshore flow. Tidal anomalies of two to three
feet are expected as a result, depending on the exact track and
strength of the low. Something around two feet above normal
would result in widespread minor tidal flooding, with moderate
in the favored vulnerable areas from Annapolis to Straits Point,
and perhaps DC/Alexandria. Anomalies closer to three feet could
result in more widespread moderate tidal flooding, with minor
even possible in spots that typically flood much less frequently
(i.e. shoreline in Cecil, Prince William, Prince Georges and
Fairfax Counties). The storm should move quickly enough to
preclude major flooding anywhere.

The heaviest rain may coincide with high tide around southern
Maryland, furthering the flooding risk due to drainage issues
along the coast with fresh plus tidal input on Thursday.

Winds shift around to the west and southwest Thursday night into
Friday, which isn't the most favorable for water to quickly 
evacuate the bay. Given the high astronomical tides (full moon 
occurred Tuesday/Nov 24), this could keep a risk of minor to
even moderate tidal flooding in the picture through Friday night.

&&

.LWX WATCHES/WARNINGS/ADVISORIES...

     for ANZ534-543.

&&
